utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I just need a minute. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you agree, with your leave, I'd like to deal with July [as interpreted] 1995 -- or, rather, with the year 1995 now. Let's see what your understanding was with regard to the year 1995, what conclusions you draw about that year. Are you aware of the fact that in Sarajevo the Muslim side launched a large-scale offensive on the 15th [as interpreted] of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was one of many offensives that the Bosnian Muslims had launched that year. One was in the zone of the 2nd Corps, one was in the zone of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see 1D2985. Perhaps it has been admitted already. 1D2985. Have you ever seen this document? Did you come across this document on the 17th of July? According to this document UNPROFOR and its services provided information on a large-scale offensive in the vicinity of Sarajevo, and you can see the contents on page number 1. Have a look at that. And on page number 2, you can see other details about this. So you're aware of this. You knew about it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the sense again I didn't see this specific document or I don't recall seeing it, but certainly I'm aware of the fact that at that particular time the Bosnian 1st Corps was launching major military operations out of the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I see Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Excuse me. Just that the document is dated 17 June. Mr. Karadzic said -- or the transcript says 17 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted? I see it's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you come across any documents according to which the 28th Division under Naser Oric's command, although he wasn't in the enclave, launched large-scale offensives against the Serbian territories in order, amongst other things, to assist the 1st Corps in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I wouldn't categorise them as large-scale offensives. However, I am aware, and I have seen documents that reflect that the 28th Division was ordered by 2nd Corps to conduct raids and other attacks out of the enclave for the primary purpose of engaging the Bosnian Serb military forces in that area in order to prevent them from being transferred from the Srebrenica area to the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see 1D3900, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you can see here, the 2nd Corps is congratulating the 28th Division command, and in particular the 285th Brigade, on successfully having undertaken action which aided in raising the blockade of Sarajevo and so on and so forth. In paragraph number four it says: "Take all steps to prevent people from leaving the area of Srebrenica and Zepa. Which for you at this moment is one of the most important task if not the most important one," et cetera. So it says that the aggressor forces, the Serb forces control the Caparde and Kladanj axis or roads. Is this what you had in mind and were you aware of -- of this matter, of the fact that they were congratulated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe -- I believe I saw this document previously, I believe, if I'm correct, during the Tolimir trial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D5542.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that here the president of the municipality, of the Muslim municipality, Suljic, Osman Suljic, agreed to launching a campaign on the 1st of July, 1995. He said he agreed to that and that he would accept everything that was stated in his name.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you refer to in the phrase of "launching a campaign" on 1st July. I assume given that we're talking about psychological and propaganda activities, we're talking about some form of a media or propaganda campaign, but certainly it is an endorsement by that individual of whatever that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this psychological and propaganda activity was directed against the Serbs and against the United Nations. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could it be adopted -- admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2234, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see D1062. D1062. It's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do we agree that this is dated the 30th of June? It's an operations report on what they did in order to help with the raising of the blockade of Sarajevo. They eliminated 13 Chetniks or, rather, Serbs. They confiscated weapons. Under item 2 it says they eliminated 7 Chetniks, obtained a significant amount of weapons. Three, it says in order to divert enemy forces from the Sarajevo theatre and stretch them out towards Srebrenica and Zepa, a number of successful acts of sabotage were carried out on the 26th of June, 1995, at the following locations: In the area of Han Pijesak and Vlasenica municipalities, 20 to 40 kilometres deep inside territory temporarily occupied by the enemy; Visnjica settlement and Bajta [phoen] stronghold, Crna Rijeka area. Do we agree that in Crna Rijeka area the Main Staff of the VRS was there? In fact, the man staff of the VRS was located in Crna Rijeka; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To get to both of your questions, yes, I agree with your interpretation of the document as to what it's describing. It is recounting a series of raids by members of the 28th Division against Bosnian Serb military installations or other villages, and I also agree that Crna Rijeka was the headquarters of the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at paragraph 3. It says that 40 Serbs were killed there and they have information according to which the Serbs had a total of 71 soldiers who were killed. One was captured and several -- a certain amount of livestock was also confiscated. And in the village of Visnjica, if you remember this, they admitted that civilians were victims. Do you remember the name of that village, Visnjica, and that date, the 26th of June?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again I am familiar with that. Not all of the specifics, but I am familiar with that particular reference being mentioned in a number of Bosnian Serb military documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if there's questions on this document I wonder if Mr. Butler could also see page 2 and see who signed it and get an idea of the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you remember that when Naser Oric was absent, Ramiz Becirevic replaced him as staff commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He was the acting commander of the 28th Infantry Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under item 4 you can see that it mentions how the Serbs, their enemy, ceased to send forces to the surroundings of Sarajevo, and they attracted some forces from Zepa and Srebrenica, and then it mentions how the fighting continued, in what manner fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, paragraph 4 relates a number of particular issues that they were talking about, and as well as some of the things that were occurring to them. So this is just simply a recap of the overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So do you remember when that order was issued, the order for combat that we had a look at yesterday, and we were wondering whether it was a matter of an operation or of combat. Was it on the 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was one of two orders that was issued on the 2nd of July, 1995, pertaining to Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see 1D5541, and I apologise if it has already been admitted, but this is the number that I have. I apologise to everyone, because the translation of this document has not yet been completed. I'll read it out and the interpreters will follow. This is the Presidency of the transitional Municipal Council of Srebrenica, dated the 9th of July. It says: "Urgent." It's being sent to Alija Izetbegovic, Haris Silajdzic, Rasim Delic the Supreme Commander, and Sead Delic the 2nd Corps commander, and it says the conclusions from the session of the Presidency, the Presidency of the municipality, with regard to the critical situation that has developed in the enclave. "On the basis of information from the 28th Division command, our lines have fallen in the southern part of the enclave in the Pusmulici sector. This has created the conditions allowing the aggressor to rapidly enter the town itself. Once that line fell, the population from Slapovici and Pusmulici moved out. There were about 4.000 of them." Mr. Butler, do you agree that these 4.000 people were previously included in the number of the population in the enclave, because this transfer of the population prior to the fighting was something that took place within the enclave itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my understanding that these 4.000 people were already residing in the enclave at the time this occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the paragraph goes on to say that: "There's general chaos in the town and the displaced -- or the refugee population is on the streets. The shelling from a number of directions which continues. No one knows how many wounded and dead there are in the town. The Muslims from Podrinje are threatened with a terrible catastrophe, and this is why we're begging you to help the people of Podrinje. Also, organise rapidly a session of the government and of the Presidency. The UNPROFOR forces in Srebrenica are panicking and trying to protect themselves. They are withdrawing towards the camp in Srebrenica, whereas one --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can save Mr. Karadzic some time in reading. We can bring up a translation. Mr. Reid's found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, so I don't have to read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they're asking the government and the Presidency to inform them by 1400 hours on the 9th of July, 1995, and it's signed by Osman Suljic, president of the interim Municipal Council of Srebrenica. Have you already come across this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I -- I mean, I -- I understand the circumstances and am familiar with that. I just don't recall if I've ever seen this particular document before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D5540. And would Mr. Nicholls be so kind as to produce the translation again if he has one -- apparently, we do have a translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the very same day, on the 9th, this was drafted a little later, probably, because he requested that a report be submitted by 2.00 p.m. Now here it says that there are no forward food reserves apart from the fact that the army has food reserves for one week. Where did the army obtain such food reserves, food reserves for one week? Would you agree that humanitarian aid in this case has been taken advantage of, that it's been put to the wrong use?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do agree. And I believe that there's been evidence, certainly in other cases I've been involved in, which reflects that the 28th Infantry Division did divert some of the UNPROFOR and other international aid to be used for the purposes of the 28th Infantry Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on that day it was in the evening after 22.20, General Krstic informed the Main Staff that he had the opportunity of liberating Srebrenica, of entering Srebrenica, and half an hour later Tolimir sent a telegram back to him with my approval. So it was only on the 9th in the evening that the Serbian forces considered the possibility of entering Srebrenica. Would you agree with that? Do you remember those documents? Perhaps I don't need to produce them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do recall the documents, and I -- again I agree with your assertion. The base Krivaja 95 operations plan does not reflect the objective of taking the town of Srebrenica, and I believe that based on the documents that you've just noted that the goal of taking the town of Srebrenica was arrived at, as you've described, on the evening of 9 April [sic] 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2236, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. Just for the transcript it says 9 April 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It should read 9 of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hope I didn't misspeak. Yes. 9 July, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you agree, I'll skip a few days to the 10th and the 11th, because your testimony and report is more important for the events that happened after those dates, from the 13th onwards; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 65 ter document 35042, please. And the number of intercept is 0415-0111. 1011, and the date is the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is of 998 pages document. Could you tell the page number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number I have is 0415/1011, but I'll find the page number now. In the meantime could we see the intercept that concerns the conversation between myself and General Zivanovic, and the date is the 8th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. No objection. Mr. Reid says that the page Mr. Karadzic is looking for for the intercept, this one, is 888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much for your help. Can we have that page called up then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we don't have English translation for it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. 0415-1011. That would be the right number. So this isn't it. 12th of June -- well, never mind. While we're looking for that, could we please have the intercept from the 8th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's tab 26, if Mr. Butler needs a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have exhibit number, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where Tri Sise is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that, if I'm correct, that's the recording, not intercept that Mr. Karadzic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you agree that this is a conversation in which I wish to receive a bit more information from General Zivanovic in terms of how things have been developing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that means that I did not find the regular combat reports to be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, what I would say is in the regular combat report come once every 24 hours. Obviously, as you're aware, the situation around Srebrenica was dramatically changing in a very dynamic manner every several hours, so it's unsurprising that you would - and again, as I've testified previously - call to the relevant military commander in order to fully apprise yourself of the situation as it was occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find this part here that I'm asking how the situation is evolving, I'm asking whether they're satisfied, is that the essence of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in Serbian now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is the first part. The second part of the conversation is that General Zivanovic uses this conversation as an opportunity to raise with you the fact that he believes he, and in this sense the Drina Corps because he's referring both to General Zivanovic and, of course, his Chief of Staff, General Krstic, will need additional forces to continue forward, and the second part of the discussion reflects not only your awareness of what forces they're talking about but the fact that they're currently deployed in other operations around Sarajevo. So it is a two-part conversation in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that at the time shells were falling in Pale? That's where I lived. That's where my daughter was getting married around the middle of that month. Do you know that Pale is part of Sarajevo and that we were in danger? We were in danger of being overcome by the corps that had three or four times more soldiers than we did.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that Pale is often referred to as Serb Sarajevo. I understand the military situation that was occurring in and around the area. I did not know, and I do not know, whether or not artillery shells fell on Pale as part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You certainly knew that before the war Pale was part of metropolitan Sarajevo, one of the ten municipalities that it consisted of.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take -- I take it that's the case. Prior to the war in this respect, I mean, I don't -- I did know very little about how Bosnia-Herzegovina was organised politically of that nature, so again I take you at your word that Pale was -- was what it was part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Yes. We have it in English now towards the bottom of the page. I am saying: "Tell me, will it continue tomorrow?" Do you agree that I'm actually putting a question, not issuing an order? In the English version it is the fifth or sixth or seventh line from the bottom "Tell me, will it continue tomorrow?"

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, in the context of this conversation, you are both requesting information and issuing orders. I mean, several lines above that you issue the phrase "All right, General. Full speed ahead. Tell Krstic to go full steam." So -- and in this conversation you are both requesting information and receiving information as well as giving direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be more correct to say that I was supporting their decisions? First I receive information as to what it was that they had decided from an operative and tactical point of view, and then I give support; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of how the operation existed at that time, and it was written in the operations planned for Krivaja, the fact that the military commanders would independently make the decisions with respect to what axis of advance they wanted to utilise and what forces they would be deploying that were already under their control, I agree. They were advising you of what their intentions were, and then you were endorsing them. They didn't -- they didn't have to advise you of what your -- their intentions were in this case, because they were already empowered to conduct those operations. So they were keeping you informed, and you were endorsing those actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, where can we find the phrase "full speed ahead" in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe I said -- I hope I said "full steam ahead." If you -- from the bottom of the second page of the English language translation it is ten lines up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because you said above that line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I got my pages mixed up. I was looking at page 2 and it's ten lines up from the bottom, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So after all, it appears after that inquiry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Will it continue."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, I say: "All right. I have heard somewhere that they were fleeing, going somewhere." Do you agree that this bit where I say "I've heard somewhere" means that they were not the ones who informed me but that I happened to hear something somewhere?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, all I can infer is what you've just said, that you happened to hear something somewhere. I can't infer whether it was through contacts with the military, and as I noted previously, you were receiving information from the police forces as well as the RDB. So you certainly had opportunities to hear information like that. Like I said, all I can infer is that from some source you heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see the next part where I say -- actually, he is saying something about Gvero and the public, and I say after that: "All right. Have someone prepare these instructions for journalists, and I am going to approve --" I don't know. I refer to the minister or something. Well, you did notice all of this, didn't you, that it was necessary to provide accurate information to journalists? Did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In fact, when you take this intercept and couple it with a document that I believe I discussed during my direct testimony, the context of this discussion is providing information to Serbian journalists in Vlasenica and Milici for the purpose of their transmission on the airwaves because they understand that the Bosnian Muslims inside the enclave monitor those news reports. And again, I look at this as part of the propaganda portion of the military operation where the discussion relates to seeking to create a climate among the Bosnian Muslims that there is no need for them to fight. They can either flee or surrender, and that is what I take this part of the conversation to be because it does marry up with another document from -- that I -- that chronologically comes down the line to discuss just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether the US Army allows enemy journalists to get close to the front line, or is it CNN or somebody else who receives favourable treatment and is allowed to report from the front line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I am certainly not an authority on -- on US military media policies. I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please take a look at -- actually, let us try to see or establish or see what you established in relation to prisoners of war. 35042 would be the 65 ter number, page 937. I don't know if we have a translation. It's short anyway, so I'll read it out to you. Do you know -- or actually, did you see any of these intercepts that the Croatian Secret Service recorded at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe we have this somewhere, Your Honour. This looks familiar to me. I'll try to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we should have. But in the meantime, could you read it, Mr. Karadzic, given it is very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. This is the 13th of July, 1995, at 11.25. "Colonel Ljubo Beara, Main Staff of the VRS is sending the following to Kasaba, four buses, two trucks, and one trailer truck to transport Muslim captives. They will be sent to the camp in Batkovici where 'selection' will be carried out distinguishing between war criminals and ordinary soldiers." You will be able to find the English translation. Did you know that Beara at 11.25 sent to Kasaba four buses, two trucks, and one trailer truck along with this order showing his intention to have the prisoners sent to Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: D2197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. To the answer to your first question, I am aware of this intercept. I am aware of what it says. However, I'm also aware that it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh. Mr. Butler, let's take it step-by-step, minute by minute if necessary. Let us see when the situation changed. In your opinion, how many prisoners were there in Nova Kasaba? Actually, not in your opinion. What was it that you established, not taking into account statements or, rather, the bragging of those who were taking prisoners. How many people were there at the stadium in Nova Kasaba on the basis of aerial images and so on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never done a calculation as to looking at that block of individuals in Nova Kasaba and trying to make a determination as to how many people that actually might be at that time. I don't have the necessary skills to do that. I'm not sure whether the investigation has or has not done that. My accounting for the number of people at various locations is on the basis of the intercepted communications by individuals who were dealing with those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we were to call up an image, if you don't take my word for this, we're going to call up an image. I did the counting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could we move into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if you do not trust me, then we can call up an aerial image. The 13th of July at 1430 hours at the stadium in Nova Kasaba there is a group of prisoners of war. Eleven lines times 7, less than 100, and on the sides there are probably senior commanders. That's an additional 100 to 150 men. So this number from the aerial image, does it tally with the capacity of the vehicles mentioned here, the buses, trucks. Would 1.000 or 2.000 people fit into these vehicles that Beara is sending to Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, one, it's a big compound question. And I have some, but this one, I think, has too many parts. And I think that we -- to understand the question, we need to see the aerial to know were these 7 lines by 11 and senior commanders, et cetera, are being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. While I have no doubt Mr. Butler would be capable of answering a compound question, but it's prudent to upload the aerial image first and then let's proceed one by one. Let's proceed one by one, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the other party help us identify the number. It's the video, Srebrenica video trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Butler, I want to tell you what my position is. I condemn the killing of a single man unless in combat, but even when people get killed in combat, I feel sorry. It would be better if they were only wounded. However, what I'm challenging here is this game of numbers that is immensely dangerous for peace in the Balkans. These exaggerations are tenfold or so. I believe that you would be the right witness through whom we can establish the truth, because you dealt with this case. So for the sake of providing you with this information, I'm trying to tell you that I'm not an insensitive man, and I condemn each and every killing, but let us see how many killings occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is not a time for your argument. It's Exhibit P4308. It's page 28 in hard copy and probably 38 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. I just thought that I should do this because of Mr. Butler. I don't want to think that I'm defending someone. I'm not defending anyone. I just want to establish what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, is this that stadium?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we zoom in a bit, the stadium itself, the central part. Actually, sorry. Before that let's take a look at this. It says 13th of July, 1995, 1400 hours; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's approximately 1400 hours is how it's labelled.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we zoom in a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Butler, that here in this aerial image we can see each and every individual. Obviously it is guards who are standing in front of. There are four plus two of them. And now please do make an effort and kindly note that there are 11 lines here times 7, in the central part of this image. So does this look like thousands of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, with all due respect, I don't believe that, it's certainly not my eyesight, but that image quality that we're looking at -- that I'm looking at right now gives me the ability to either confirm or deny your number count. I -- I can't tell. I mean, you've given a number of what you believe it looks like. I can't tell off the quality of this image that I'm looking at right now whether -- whether you're correct or whether you're not correct, sir. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go back to the total now. Do you agree that a provincial football stadium would not be longer than 60 or 70 metres and would not be wider than 40 metres? This is certainly not Wembley Stadium, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. But I -- again, being an American, maybe I'm kind of missing the point on this, but doesn't it have to be somewhere at least about 100 metres long? I mean, isn't that the point of the game? I mean, I have no idea. I've never walked the measurement of how big or how long Nova Kasaba stadium may or may not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No way, not 100 metres. Eighty metres are the best fields and this is a lot less. Do you see now how big the area is where the prisoners are standing? Can we speak of thousands here? Can we even speak of hundreds in the plural?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, what would I tell you is that looking at this particular image, one, I can't -- from an image without any form of an index on it that allows you to estimate scale, I can't tell you how big or how small Nova Kasaba football field is. I suppose one could do a rough analysis by taking a measurement of a known object like a vehicle or a house and then you could extrapolate that. And I again also can tell you that based on the image I'm looking at, I can't give you a number. If I were to take a number off of -- off of the top of my head, looking at that clump of individuals in the centre as well as the lines on the side, my ballpark estimate would be several hundred at this point in time. I would also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. No objection, just if Mr. Karadzic wants to, I would let him know that the page earlier, wider, has vehicles and other reference points that Mr. Butler [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going on, I know your position is that the number itself is not critical or relevant, but do you have any position as to the number of prisoners that are shown in this aerial image on the part of the Prosecution, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, not an exact number, Your Honour. However, the intercept at 1402 says more than a thousand down here at the stadium. I -- my position would be that without more expert analysis, we can't tell. This could, in my submission, be a thousand or more, especially if you look at the wider angle and you can see the buses. It may be something that he should be able to do the measurements and call an expert if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we show him the previous page. Did you refer to this page, Mr. Nicholls, or after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is the one just if Mr. Karadzic wishes, because the witness brought up a question about vehicles, and here you can see some actual vehicles on the road.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we have a look, we can see two buses. How long is a normal bus, an ordinary bus, Mr. Butler, if you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't, sir. I have no idea how long a normal bus is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this bus with the length it is could fit two or three busloads when lined up next to this group of prisoners, maybe even more than three? We could measure, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's with a we have to do, I can do it the old fashioned way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This bus on this scale is 6 millimetres long. Let's not change it. And here the length of this group 15 millimetres. So less than three buses --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it that first block of individuals, the lengthwise is two buses and the scale going up is one and roughly one-quarter bus. So what does that measure out to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many people can fit, these people here, obviously, sitting? How many people can sit down in an area like this. In this large group, it's less than 100, 11 times 7.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea how many people could fit in a space that size, sir. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I'm just speaking for myself, but this seems to be pretty unproductive to engage in this -- what is no more than speculation. Now, there are so many variables. I mean, how big are the people? How close are they sitting together? It doesn't really help.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellency. I will leave this topic, but I'm just trying to say that these things are more objective than my bragging on the telephone about what a hero I am and how many people I captured. We have information that Beara is sending two trucks and a trailer --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and we have on the other hand the bragging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'd like to give testimony yourself, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll see. Maybe at the end I will testify. Let us look at P4532.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are still on the 13th of July, which is very important. Look, please. On the 13th of July at 13.55, and we will see that on the reception stamp, at 11.25, Beara sends the means of transport, and at 13.55, the Main Staff issues this order. And in the preamble it says: "Based on the instructions received and following the defeat suffered in the Srebrenica enclave, the able-bodied men from the enclave fit for military service were tasked with crossing over to Tuzla and Kladanj in groups -- in groups and carrying weapons. Among them are inveterate criminals and villains who will stop at nothing just to avoid being captured and reach Muslim-controlled territory." The text below talks about the taking of prisoners, and the order says: "The corps command and brigade commands shall engage all available men fit for military service to detect, block, disarm, and capture detected Muslim groups and prevent them from crossing over to the Muslim territory. Along the whole road, Zvornik, Crni Vrh, Sekovici, Vlasenica. Organise ambushes, et cetera. "2. In Serbian villages on the axis of the group's movement protect and secure the people. "3. Detain the captured and disarmed Muslims in appropriate facilities that can be secured by fewer troops. Immediately report to the superior command." So at half past 1.00, the intention of the Main Staff is to place the captured people in facilities that do not need large security details, and the superior commands are to be informed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next point in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Point 6: "Through the competent authorities and Ministry of the Interior make sure that all available manpower is engaged in the co-ordinated execution of the above-said tasks." Do you recall, Mr. Butler, that you noted yourself that the army realized all the seriousness of the threat posed by these groups only on the 13th? Only then did they realise how large these groups were and their capacity to break through and inflict losses on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There was that period, as I've discussed earlier, where the Main Staff and the senior officers were discounting the initial reports from the field as to the size of the column that had been able to successfully cross the Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba road and proceed north into the Zvornik Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Butler, that from the 11th to the 14th, I was preoccupied only with establishing the civilian authorities in Srebrenica, issuing orders to appoint a civilian commissioner to establish a police station, to provide protection and security for people and property? Until the 15th, I had no information about the dangers. Have you found a single document warning me of danger?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The danger of what, sir? You used the phrase "danger." What do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the same context. The danger posed by the 28th Division, which is in the sector between Srebrenica and Tuzla, our sector, the one we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So I just wanted to be clear because the way that you predicated your question, I just thought for a second that you were referring to the danger of the prisoners being killed, and I just wanted to make sure I'm clear on what I'm answering. The military documents reflect that by the afternoon of the 14th, that the military commands are starting to become more aware of this, that by the evening of the 14th, they're already giving orders to start to remove forces from Zepa that will start going out the morning of the 15th. I can't agree with your first assertion that you were solely preoccupied with establishing the civilian authorities in Srebrenica because I believe that the army must have co-ordinated with you and sought your permission to begin all of the things that they needed to do in order to begin a major military operation against the Zepa enclave. So that is something that had to have been briefed to you by the army with respect to what was happening down there, and I believe you would have had to have approved that before the army would have undertaken that. I also believe that on the 13th, while the army may not have been reporting it, certainly Mr. Dragomir Vasic - in his reports up the police chain of command to the police staff - and the RDB were providing reports as to what they believed the seriousness of the military situation was, and unlike the Main Staff, Dragomir Vasic did believe that the military situation that was developing was far more serious than the army had taken account for. So I can't speak to you what you did or did not know on a certain time, but what I do believe is that even if the army was down playing or did not recognise themselves the gravity of the military threat to Zvornik, I believe that the threat to Zvornik was properly manifested by the reports that Mr. Vasic was forwarding and other reports that were coming up the police and the RDB chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler -- yes. I was waiting for the French and B/C/S translation to be completed. Did you find any VRS Main Staff report or MUP report that went to the president dealing with the danger of the column before 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Main Staff reports do go to the president, and I believe they talked about it on the 15th. The MUP reports from Vasic go as high as the police staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The MUP report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proper MUP report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not CSB in Zvornik or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reports that were done by Mr. Vasic went to the police staff. I do not know if -- and I cannot talk about how they may have gone further up the chain of command to President Karadzic at that juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that in the regular combat reports they say that certain groups of fighters are surrendering to the VRS, and they don't see the situation as dangerous, so they don't report it to me as dangerous; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, they are talking about -- and I believe the point in time we're talking about now is the 13th and 14th period, you see a number of military reports where they do routinely talk about the apprehension of large numbers of prisoners. Those are incorporated in, I think, one or two Main Staff reports that go to you. There are no numbers associated with it, but it reflects, you know, large numbers. But there is nothing in the Main Staff reporting to you that I take away that the VRS believes that having these prisoners in their custody is somehow dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you come up with that, Mr. Butler? Let's stick to the chronology. I'm asking you did the army warn me that there was something extraordinary and unusual before the 14th of July? Well, let's put it differently. Do you know that on the 14th of July I declared the state of war in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On the 14th of July, 1995, you issued a decree declaring a state of war to exist in the Srebrenica municipality. That does not include Bratunac, and it does not include the Zvornik municipality. It's solely that, the Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that I did not do that at the prompting of the army but after I visited the civilian authorities of Bratunac, Srebrenica, and Skelani, who informed me that any of these towns may fall if the 28th Division decides to act?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said "after I visited the civilian authorities." Are you referring to you physically visited the civilian authorities of these individuals prior to issuing that decree, or is that a translation issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It must be interpretation. Do you know that on the 14th of July, I received a visit of the delegation of the civilian authorities of Bratunac, Srebrenica, and Skelani, and among them was the civilian commissioner Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some memories of Deronjic in his statement, but I'm not aware of other individuals visiting you, so I mean I guess the fairest answer I can give on that is I'm not aware of the visits that you had on 14 July. They're not -- they're not in the military documents and other material I would work at -- I mean, I'm generally not aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber is aware of this, as is the OTP, all about this 14th of July. Did you wonder why, prompted by what, Karadzic declared the state of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My presumption of your declaration of a state of war and the establishment of a war Presidency for the municipality of Srebrenica was for you and for the municipal authorities to gain a better -- or gain better control of the then chaotic situation in the town of Srebrenica as part of the process of re-establishing Serbian political and civilian control over the town, restarting the utilities. Those declarations give the War Presidency additional extraordinary powers that they can use in order to assist in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that in these orders and decrees the decisions relate to the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica? Did you make any conclusion as to the meaning of this? What does that mean, the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't draw any conclusion one way or another about that, sir. It's the municipality of Srebrenica. The fact that after the Serbs occupied or liberated the municipality they would call it the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica, it seems natural to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you that before the war an agreement was reached that in mixed municipality, two municipalities would be set up, one Serbian and one Muslim. In many places, written agreements were signed. Is it the case that on the 11th of July I appointed a commissioner for the Serbian part of Srebrenica, now that you know there were supposed to be two municipalities? It says Deronjic was appointed for the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the -- I don't know the -- your first assertion, so I can't comment on what agreement may or may not have been made during the war. I assume that when you talk about this, you know, your appointment of Mr. Deronjic for the municipality of Srebrenica. If there was a Muslim municipality of Srebrenica in existence on 12 and 13 of July, it would have been a very empty place. There was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could I request a cite, please, to the written agreement to divide Srebrenica into two municipalities, if there is one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I will lead evidence of that, but we already know that negotiations did take place, and it's obvious that I held it to be true on the 11th that there would be two municipalities. However, the negotiations took place before the war in all municipalities. In Bratunac an agreement was signed. I'm just trying to see if this expert knows why my decrees apply to the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We heard the answer. So you referred to the one in Bratunac. That's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The Bratunac one I understand. I was asking about Srebrenica. A separate municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agreement was not signed for Srebrenica, but the agreement was reached. It existed, and we will show that. I believe it's already been shown. Could we now look briefly at P04460.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look, please. Can we see item 6, which relates to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 15th July. The Main Staff informs me several groups have surrendered. Is this supposed to alarm me that several groups had surrendered? There is no mention of the number or any warning of danger. On the 15th, I'm being notified that several groups have surrendered. I'll find it in a moment. Yes. It says: "Earlier today, several enemy groups have surrendered to members of the VRS in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade." Have you found it? [In English] "During the course of today's day, several enemy groups have surrendered to the VRS members."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this supposed to alarm the president of the republic, who has a thousand other things to do, or is this just regular information in keeping with your own conclusion that the army was not aware of the seriousness of the situation or the threat posed by the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer -- this is a two-part question. Let me answer the second part first. If you look at this in time sequence as to when this document was published, you can tell from parts of the language that they are an incorporating Colonel Pandurevic's interim combat report on the 15th of July, 1995. So this is part of that reporting chain up. The second issue is I would again note that the military was not your only mechanism to receive information, particularly information that would potentially alarm you. I recall that on the 15th of July, 1995, there is an RDB report from the Zvornik municipality which reports over a hundred prisoners have escaped from a facility in Pilica. Even though it turns out that that report was ultimately erroneous, I would think that a report noting that a hundred prisoners of war had escaped would raise some alarm at some levels of the police leadership and may have ultimately reached you. So again my point is while I cannot comment on what information you may or may not have actually known at any given time, you were not solely dependent upon the military to ascertain what was going on in any given area. From the armed -- the other components of the armed forces, you did have the police reporting -- or at least the police staff had the police reporting and Minister Kovac had the police reporting as well as the RDB reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one question if I may. Do you agree that the army and the police have a rivalry between them, and I should be informed of military issues by the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the military had many issues with the police forces, in part because members of the MUP were being paid regular salaries while most members of the army were not, and as a result that led to significant morale issues as well as soldiers deserting to the MUP whenever they thought they could get a job there. I agree with your assertion that military report on military matters, police will report on police matters. I will also remind you that at the times that we're talking about these reports, most of the police forces, even though they were under the control of the army - they had been resubordinated for the operations - they were still continuing to report those military operations up the police chain. And finally, as noted in the RDB reporting, the RDB itself did not limit itself to reporting on just police issues. They also reported on their understanding of the military issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The question about this document, page 32, lines 15 to 19, just to summarise, was -- there's nothing in here which -- which should alarm the president who is so busy with a thousand things to do. The army was not aware of the seriousness of the situation or the threat posed by the 28th division. If that's being put to the witness, I think he should be allowed to look at the entire section on the situation in the zone of the Drina Corps before answering on what this report says. This is at your tab 102, Mr. Butler, but I don't think -- I think he needs to see the whole section before it's put to him that nothing here is alarming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show him the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I can just clarify something. I was referring to Mr. Butler's finding according to which the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Having seen the remainder of the document, would you like to add anything, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you look at the second page of the document, it also notes the situation on the territory, that there -- not only -- the most alarming part that I would look at, of course, would be the fact that major roads, the Vlasenica-Zvornik road is un-safe due to the enemy groups which are seeking to break out. From a civil point of view that certainly would be of relevance to the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Let us leave at it that. But before we break there is one matter I want to deal with. The Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's bar table motion for the admission of documents related to the hostages component with appendix A which was filed on the 18th of April, 2012. This motion includes the accused's submission in relation to each of the document. So, Mr. Robinson, I take it therefore that the Defence is not going to file a further response. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We would like to be heard since the Prosecution has given its rationale for why those particular objections ought to be disregarded. We would like to be heard at least on some of them before the Trial Chamber makes a decision, so we planned on filing a response to that motion as well as the other bar table motions that will be coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The crux is that you would like to reply to the response of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we would like to respond to the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what's the point of incorporating Defence response in that motion itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the process that we have going right now is so that both parties can be aware of the position of the other party before the motion is made to the Chamber. And so when we put in a little box in that column our objection, we're not really stating a full legal argument, but then the Prosecution when it files its motions is making their legal argument as to the relevance of those things. So we think that we ought to have the opportunity to inform the Chamber more fully and more formally as to the basis of our objections when we have a dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When can I expect to have your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Given the time, we'll take a break now. We'll have a break for 30 minutes and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, for planning purposes, the Chamber is minded to rise for this session at quarter past 12.00, and instead sit a bit longer period than usual in the third session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I believe that you noticed that the Prosecution took more than eight hours, and if we take into account the material that is being admitted through this witness and the reports, I would need a little more time than the time that was allocated to the Prosecution -- or, rather, used by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Prosecution did not use all the eight hours that they estimated, but notwithstanding that, as long as you stay on relevant issues, the Chamber is minded to give some leeway, but -- that's -- again, I emphasise you should be focused and stay on relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I appreciate that. Could the witness please be shown D2212.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's something I'd like to clarify, Mr. Butler. I asked you about reports according to which some groups should surrender. Should such reports be a matter of concern for the president? Should they alarm the president, or were such reports submitted as a matter of course?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't speak to the issue of alarm, but within the context of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, historically the documents that I have reviewed reflect a great interest by the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership to exchange prisoners that they had taken in order to get prisoners from -- who -- to get Bosnian Serbs who had been imprisoned in Muslim prisons, either captured or for a variety of other reasons. So the issue of prisoner exchanges did receive the highest level attention of the Republika Srpska government, including you personally, and there's documents which, of course, reflect that. Regardless of the numbers that are in dispute, the fact is that hundreds if not thousands of prisoners were falling into the custody of the army -- or I should be more clear, the armed forces of Republic Srpska because it was not just the army, it was the police forces as well, from the period of 12 July onward through at least the 22nd of July. And those numbers of prisoners would have dramatically changed the calculations and the leverage that the Republika Srpska would have had in order to retrieve those Bosnian Serbs who were imprisoned by the Muslims. So in that respect, I believe that the issues of prisoners of war would have been of great importance to the senior military and political leadership of the country, the pinnacle of that being you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please have a look at the report from Doctors Without Borders. I don't know whether this document can be broadcast. I don't see that it's marked as a Rule 50 document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be scrolled up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, we have a report from Doctors Without Borders on the events, but what I want to show you is the part where it says that Mladic is in Bratunac and he is offering food and water. Let me just find that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to let you know, Mr. Karadzic, this is just -- this is a public document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see page 5. I'm looking at the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is a report for the 11th of July in which all the events are described. Franken the deputy commander was at a meeting. They were co-operating productively and so on and so forth. And then it's the second paragraph towards the end, it says: [In English] Commandant Mladic BSA is in Bratunac and offering medicine and food, asks UN to organise buses for evacuation." [Interpretation] He's saying that the UN could organise the buses. This is at 22.50, and it's after the second meeting that was held in the Fontana Hotel; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I take it from the time on this and the context of what was discussed, the Dutch -- I guess it was Major Franken at the time, was back briefing this particular individual as to what the results of that meeting were and how it would impact that organisation. So that is at least the first part under where it looks to be "News."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have a brief look at P4769. Can we agree that this is a telegram from General Tolimir that was delivered at 22.30, and it says: "If you are unable to find adequate accommodation for all POWs from Srebrenica, we hereby inform you that space has been arranged for 800 prisoners of war in the first plpbr in Sjemec." It says they could work on the farm and General Tolimir on the 13th of July offers accommodation for 800 prisoners. He found a place where they could be provided with accommodation. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I testified with relation to this document in the Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It doesn't look like Tolimir wants them to be there so that they could be killed. It seems more like he wants them to be able to live there so that they could work on the farm; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with your assertion on that because it is my awareness that at the time in question this particular farm, in fact, was not a working farm. I believe that in the Tolimir case that there was information that suggested that nobody was using this particular farm at the time. If that is in fact the case, I don't believe that that was a genuine assertion by General Tolimir that they would be working on agricultural projects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I think that your answer doesn't show that you are unbiased. Do you know that there was a farm for sheep, horses, and pigs there, and what would have enabled the army to live had there not been such a farm? This is a confidential telegram. It's not a propaganda leaflet. So I really have the impression that you are striving to assist the Prosecution. You're fighting for the Prosecution's side, and you won't admit certain facts that are quite clear in this document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, again, I can tell you I understand what the document says, and I can tell you that I'm testifying with respect to that particular paragraph on the basis of knowledge that I have about the situation as it's been described at that farm. If I am incorrect or if there is other evidence, I expect the Trial Chamber will take that of note, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to this document, my question is whether Tolimir is saying they should be killed, or is he saying that accommodation should be provided? And I'm not asking you about your opinion. I'm interested in the facts themselves.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. I agree with you in that particular context. He is not saying that they're going to be killed. And I guess when I testified about this document in the Tolimir case, the thing that struck me the most about it was it is one of the few documents that I'm aware of that actually assigns a number of prisoners. In this particular case it's talking about 800 prisoners of war. So again in the correlation of trying to determine how many prisoners are in the custody of the VRS and of the MUP at various points of time during the whole Srebrenica crime base review, I found this to be a very interesting document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Could we now see 65 ter document 31023, and it's half an hour later. 65 ter number 31023B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there was even a farm in Crna Rijeka near the Main Staff, and it had been established by the army. This doesn't relate to this document, but I'm just asking you whether you were aware of the fact that there were military farms whenever that was possible. Did you know that there was a farm in Crna Rijeka next to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer the first question, yes, sir, I'm aware of the practice that, where possible, military units had their own farms in order to provide sustenance and other support to the brigade. I did not know that there was a farm in Crna Rijeka that was -- that belonged to the Main Staff or belonged to the military there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's have a look at this intercept. It doesn't have to be broadcast. I don't know whether it's public or not. It's 602. It says at -- on the 13th at 2005, a conversation between General Mladic and a certain Ljubo was recorded, and we couldn't hear him. Is it reasonable to assume that the Ljubo in question was, in fact, Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is -- I believe I've testified to that related to this intercept in previous cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it says here that Mladic spoke on the phone, and he thought that it was a safe line. Obviously it wasn't. Mladic ordered Beara and suggested that they provide food. He said that there should be sufficient food. He should see where it could be found, and he should obtain food so that the people were not hungry.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Yes, sir. Yes, sir. That's what it says. Is there another question, or did I miss a question? I apologise if I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to ask you whether that's what you can see in the intercept. And when you compiled your report, did you have this intercept in mind? Did you refer to this intercept in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again, I've testified to this as well. There are multiple meanings that one might infer from this intercept. As a matter of being conservative, I think in most cases - I hope in all cases - what I've noted is the fact that there are a lot of police forces out there that are in those particular areas, and as noted by the laws of the Republika Srpska with respect to the Ministry of the Interior, that it is the responsibility of the army to feed and provision the MUP forces that are operating under their command in various areas. So at its most benign interpretation, Beara is raising the point that there are police officers there who have not been fed. They don't have their own logistics. And Mladic is making it known, Yes, solve it so that there's no food problems. And he's talking about giving an order to Krle, which would be the Drina Corps, to ensure that that happens and bring the stuff over to Malinic's. That would logically be a place to bring food and be able to further distribute to the police forces. There's clearly a more sinister way to look at this as well, but I don't think I need to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last part of the question is whether you referred to this intercept in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, with all due respect, your interpretations are really quite odd. How do you see that it concerns the police? How could the policemen remain hungry? [In English] Excellent. Just keep working and feed them all. There are a lot of hungry mouths." [Interpretation] Why would the police be hungry? This concerns prisoners, Mr. Butler. And Beara, who was a security officer, why would he be responsible for providing food for the police since this is a matter for logistics, not for security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the reason I mention that is particularly with the intercepts, some of them are open to multiple interpretations. My practice when analysing both military documents, as well as the intercepts, as a matter of fairness on the issue was if there were multiple interpretations, I would lean towards giving it an interpretation that had the most -- or the best military context. I don't necessarily disagree with your interpretation of this. However, in the context of my previous testimony where many of these individuals were accused of this, your interpretation effectively at this point, you know, notes that Colonel Beara and General Mladic are aware that there are a large number of prisoners, that they are hungry. The guidance is that solve it so there is no lack of food. And if one looks at the end result, they did. That is not an interpretation that I believe I could make before various Trial Chambers on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the 13th at 11.00. Don't confuse --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object to him cutting off the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can ask a question at any time, Mr. Karadzic. Do not interrupt while the witness is answering a question, Mr. Karadzic. Will you continue, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, sir, I completed my answer at that point. That was my last comment. I didn't believe that I could make that type of an interpretation of this intercept before the various tribunals that I testified before, given the context of the accused who were in the stand at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you believe that Mladic and Beara were not discussing about feeding the prisoners in real sense.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, what I believe is there are two interpretations to this. And as a matter of fairness, I assigned this -- in my analytical review of the material, I'm noting for the Trial Chamber that there are two possible interpretations, and again to be conservative, I believe that, you know, from my perspective the most conservative interpretation is potentially a discussion related to the police forces who are there, who would be dependent on the military for resupply, including food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The reason for that was because of the end result.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The reason for such belief on your part, was it due to the end result, as you stated earlier on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again, sir, if I were to give it the second interpretation, then it would, of course, radically change the meaning of the comment, "solve it so there is no lack of food."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As indicated by Mr. Karadzic. Would it not be possible that while they were discussing about real feeding, but they changed their mind afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe so, because if one were then to go back and look at the corresponding Bratunac Brigade documents, it is absolutely clear that there are no orders given as reflected in the documents to start providing food and other provisions to these prisoners. Given the numbers of individuals that are falling into military custody on the 13th of July, even if I use a minimum number in the morning of perhaps a thousand, the Bratunac Brigade itself only had 3.000 -- 3.500 soldiers at the time. So that is a significant percentage in terms of the food reserves that the Bratunac Brigade might have. One would expect if that was in fact the case, there would be documentation and orders and perhaps even intercepts reflecting the various activities of the staff members of the Bratunac Brigade and the Drina Corps to bring truckloads of rations for all of these prisoners. I don't see that in the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you know that the Bratunac Brigade was mostly outside the area of responsibility and that it was old men who were guarding the prisoners that night in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My understanding is that the four battalions of the Bratunac Brigade were involved in various military operations. Some of them were in Potocari. Some of them that were along the load -- road from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje, and that the number of prisoners that were coming into Bratunac on 13 July 1995 greatly exceeded the ability of the remaining brigade units, which would be the military police and some of the rear services units, to guard them and that there was, in fact, a call for all able-bodied men residing in Bratunac to report for duty guarding prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
