utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know which formation or which institution provided food and water to the prisoners in Potocari and the prisoners in Sandici? Was it the brigade or was it the civilian protection? Also, did you try to find traces of feeding in the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that there was some food and some water that was brought into Potocari on the 12th. I believe that -- I'm familiar with some testimony that it came from the Bratunac Brigade, or at least the Bratunac Brigade rear services organ had a role in it. I don't know if it originated from the Bratunac Brigade or whether it came from the civilian protection services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, we had a protected witness here from the civilian protection who told us the same thing that I've been telling you; namely, that that had been their job, not the job of the rear services of the Bratunac Brigade, no way. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I don't comment on what witnesses may or may not have said. I mean, that's not my role before this Trial Chamber, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it considerably differs from what you concluded, and it actually challenges it. So the civilian protection, which is part of the armed forces, they dealt with food and water, and your expectation is that this was done by the military. Since you did not find any traces of the army providing that, you conclude that that had not been provided. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for some clarity - I'm not objecting - but providing food and water to civilians gathered in Potocari is a different thing from providing food and water to persons -- prisoners who have been taken. So I just want to know which we're talking about when the questions are put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to give a number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before that, did you say in lines 7 to 8 on this page that civilian protection is part of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. According to our laws, civilian protection is also part of the armed forces. However, they are not part of the combat units. In wartime, it is under the army or under the defence forces. It's part of the defence system. That would be the right wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take a look at what Witness 480 said, that they provided food and water to prisoners in buses and in Sandici and that that was their job. Let me ask you this now, Mr. Butler. Have you come to realise that Colonel Beara dealt with prisoners of war? Did you establish that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents establish that a -- as the chief of security for the Main Staff, one of Colonel Beara's responsibilities would have been related to issues of prisoners of war, and I believe that the evidence led through various Srebrenica-related trials here has laid out in great detail Colonel Beara's involvement in the issue of prisoners from the period 12 through the 20th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you come a cross a document that shows that Beara dealt with logistics, especially providing supplies to the police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. And again in this document I don't take it that he is going to engage in logistics issues. He's just as part of the conversation noting that. And again, orders are given over there at Krle's for material to be sent, and again in the context of the phrase "Krle," an abbreviation for General Krstic, I take that to be some orders are going out to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it hasn't been, we'll receive it now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2237, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please help us with this now: Quite simply, let us establish when most people were being taken prisoner. Until when were most people taken prisoner? Was that on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, chronologically speaking, the men start getting separated in Potocari beginning on the afternoon of the 12th. So at that point in time, I would categorise that as the start of the process where the military-aged men start to come into the custody of the armed forces, either the police or the army. As the evening of the 12th wears on and goes into the morning of the 13th, the police and military forces that were originally along the road from Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and down, start to capture significant numbers of men from the column. The numbers from the 13th are relatively apparent from intercepts and other pieces of information. I am aware that prisoners were also captured in that same area on the 14th, as well as in subsequent ways the 15th, 16th, and 17th. I would have to say, though, again I don't have a number, and I don't believe a number of prisoners captured strictly on the 14th of July along that area has -- has ever surfaced. So it's hard to say whether the peak day of prisoners being captured by the armed forces is the 13th or the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that according to our regulations, this was the procedure: Taking people prisoner, bringing them to a collection point or a collection centre, then reporting to the higher command. Is that what is written, and is that what was done in this case? I'm just talking about the 13th. I'm interested in the 13th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The process, at least as far as the military was concerned, was that upon capturing a prisoner, the prisoner was to be brought to a designated facility. He was to be safeguarded in a designated facility where he would then be -- his identity established, he would be interrogated for any potential useful combat-related information, and then ultimately turned over to the appropriate authorities where he would then be sent to the main prisoner of war holding facilities, Batkovici being one of them. On the 13th, the picture on the ground was that prisoners were being captured at various locations. They were being assembled at various areas, and I believe Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, Sandici, and there are some smaller areas where they were being assembled, and then as the 13th wore on, a large group of those prisoners were brought to the Kravica warehouse facility. Other prisoners were taken other places. I believe there's one, perhaps at least two, small-level executions which occur on the 13th of July. And then as the evening continues to wear on, of course, by 1700 the beginning of the Kravica warehouse massacre, and as the evening continues on, those prisoners who are still remaining at Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, Sandici are then put into buses and trucks and taken to other locations. Some of them were outside the Kravica supermarket in trucks. Most of them apparently were brought into the town of Bratunac on vehicles or buses and stored there, though I'm in -- I am aware of one case at Sandici where apparently after all the buses and trucks stopped there were still some prisoners and they were summarily executed at that site. So that is my recounting of what the prisoner situation looked like on 13 July 1995, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you -- I mean, if I put shorter questions, could you please give shorter answers that pertain only to what I'm asking? So is it correct that prisoners, in addition to Kravica on the 13th of July, were also brought to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in addition to Kravica and Bratunac, that is close to Kravica, there were no other collection points?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were multiple collection points in the town of Bratunac. I'm aware that prisoners were held in the town of Kravica. I do not know if on the evening of the 13th whether or not there were prisoners at Nova Kasaba or Konjevic Polje. I know they were collection sites during the day. I do not know if prisoners were stored there during the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you not see for yourself that they were all transported to Bratunac, and did you notice that the civilian authorities of Bratunac were complaining? They were saying, "You're taking them prisoner in the area of Vlasenica, Milici, Zvornik, and you're bringing all of them to Bratunac." Do you remember that that was an objection that had been raised, "Why are you bringing them all to Bratunac?"

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of the 13th of July, I agree that the civilian authorities in Bratunac were complaining about the prisoners that were all being brought to that location. And that -- it started even earlier than the 13th. Again, I can't comment as to whether those were the only locations, because I just do not know about -- prisoners were clearly being taken through the evening of the 13th and the morning of the 14th. I just have no information about whatever happened to them, because I don't know if there were any survivors of people taken prisoner at that time. I am aware also that as part of the response to that, the first convoy loads of prisoners left Bratunac at 2000 hours on 13 July. So even though the municipal authorities were planing about the spiraling number of prisoners in town, there were steps taken to at least take some of the prisoners from Bratunac and move them up to the Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So whoever was taken prisoner was in Bratunac that night. According to your findings, how many persons were involved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't say that. Again, if you -- you and I both agree there were prisoners stored at Kravica as well. So not every prisoner taken was in Bratunac that night. I don't know -- I mean, I don't know if I've ever come across an accurate number of prisoners were in Bratunac that evening. I will leave that to other people's testimony to that account. Obviously I'm not in Bratunac on that day. I can't make any firsthand observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come across the information that I had received, the extent to which they had sent information to me from Bratunac? They said that they were so burdened, they had so many prisoners on the night of the 13th. Is it correct that they said around 2.000?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number wouldn't -- wouldn't surprise me if it were 2.000. It might in fact even be more. Again, as I've noted before when you asked, I am aware of the fact that the civilian authorities in Bratunac were greatly concerned about the security issues. I know that there were issues raised in reports, but I have no information or I can't testify as to whether or not municipal authorities in Bratunac personally called you and provided you with these issues other than the one document which is purported to be a conversation between you and Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what does it say, about 2.000? And perhaps during the night there may be even more of them; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall during the night there may be even more of them. I think Mr. Deronjic does, in fact, say several thousand. I mean, I don't know if it gives the number 2.000 or just says several thousand, but again, that's why 2.000 is probably sticking in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for precision, I don't have it in front of me, but that intercept says "will be more," not "maybe."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did you notice that 2.000 was mentioned in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, is might have been actually giving the number. I just don't recall it off the top of my head right now, but I'm not disagreeing with your categorisation of the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just what's the exhibit number for that, Mr. Nicholls? Or Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am staying away from everything that has to do with Mr. Deronjic, for well-known reasons, but I think that this has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you can come back to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the Muslim authorities thought? How many inhabitants were there in Srebrenica? How many got out to Tuzla, and how many were missing? Propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 4618 to answer your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Again, the numbers of the individuals in the enclave run a range. I believe in one of the documents the Muslims actually put a number that they have. I know that the UN has had numbers. I know that the VRS believes, and they have a certain number as well. So there's a range of numbers with respect to who was in the enclave. So I can't tell you exactly what the Muslim authorities thought, how many inhabitants were there. I am not sure I know how many got to Tuzla. I think there's an accurate accounting of the women and children and elderly that were taken through the lines at Kladanj. I have heard various numbers as to how many members of the column ultimately arrived in Tuzla, but I've never done an analysis on that myself to determine whether or not it's a valid number. And as for the number of the missing, I believe -- or the dead in this particular context, I believe that that's already been the subject of testimony by forensics experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether you saw a telegram from the secret service from Tuzla dated the 17th of July, namely that on the 16th of July, 10.000 soldiers arrived in Tuzla? Of course, it goes without saying that not all of them had been armed. Ten thousand soldiers of the 28th Division. Did you take that report into account?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing a report like that. If you have it as a document to show me, I would take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we're going to call it up if we have enough time. This has already been admitted. Now I'd like to show you 1D5024. This is a record of the session of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 11th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could that please be displayed in e-court. I beg your pardon. We actually have this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can move on. This was already discussed. "Two thousand, but there will be more during the night."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now take a look at -- actually, there is a translation too. There is. Maybe it hasn't been uploaded. Could it please be placed on the ELMO then. Could you please place on the ELMO the part where it says 42.000, the response of the president, 42.000 and 35.000. [In English] For the usher. For the usher. [Interpretation] Serbian is page 6. In Serbian, it's page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here Silajdzic says -- in fact, the president asks. Then it says he knows how many soldiers there had been. And the president says, You can ask Selo to provide a report about that. Silajdzic says, Here is what it's about. First of all in Srebrenica they provided one number for UNPROFOR, and we knew another number. The president says, 42.000 for the UNPROFOR, but realistically it was 35.000.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in Serbian, please. The English can romaine the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now Silajdzic says he's afraid it's not 35 but a little more than 36.000. And 31.000-something left -- remained, actually, because 5.000 left to join friends and family, et cetera. And he says: "The most unfavourable number --" The president says: "The most unfavourable number is 5.000, meaning that nobody was excluded, isn't it?" And Silajdzic says: "I'm afraid this is right." The president says: "There is hope that there are some of them here -- here and there after all. "Some of them are in Serbia. Some run away to Serbia via Zepa and 35.000 remained. 31.000 at least had made it to Tuzla, maybe more." And then it says the number of killed is around 3.000. We intercepted a conversation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic slow down and tell us where he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters can't catch up with your speed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm in a hurry. I thought there was a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this one asks: Is it 300? And the other one says, No, add a zero, one Chetnik says to another. So, Mr. Butler, this is one month after the event, a transcript from the Presidency session where we see that there was 36.000 population in Srebrenica at most. At least 670 went to Zepa towards Serbia. At least several thousand left for Tuzla. Can you tell us how many got killed in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, I don't mean to interrupt, but just because the way the question was framed, we should go on to the next statement to put that 3.000 number that was quoted in context. It's on page 7 of the English. It's just been put that they were talking about 3.000 max as the number of dead. I won't say anything else, but Mr. Butler should be able to read the next two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. It is reckoned that there are many left in the woods, that many are still fighting. Is it consistent with your knowledge that -- that many of them remained for months in the forests fighting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I'm going to try and run through all the questions. I agree and I've testified before that even after the bulk of the column got out that there were -- there were groups sometimes numbering in the hundreds who were trapped behind the lines and as a result were wandering back there. As to your other question, no, I never did an analysis as to how many people from the column were killed as a result of the combat operations. I know that forensically in the post-conflict years those are individuals that are referred to as surface remains and that numbers of those individuals have been determined. So to back up one step, the casualties that were taken as part of the column activities in the fighting of the column, were not particularly my concern. From an analytical perspective, once I came to the conclusion myself that the column was a legitimate military target for the VRS to engage, the casualties that occurred in that column would not be considered to be casualties from the other Srebrenica-related war crimes. My goal in looking at the column, the route that the column took, and the combat that occurred was not related to the number of casualties in the column but was only done so I would be able to assist the investigation team in distinguishing where combat activities were taking place on any given day so that the team would understand where the combat operations were occurring and where the mass executions were occurring so that all concerned would understand that people in certain graves were not combat casualties because the column was nowhere near where those locations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question before the break. Do you know where in the area of which brigade in which part of that sector did the fiercest fighting take place with the greatest losses involved for both the Serbian and Muslim side? Was it in the place where the column was exiting towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two answers to that question. With respect to the Zvornik municipality, by far the largest number of casualties for the column and the Zvornik Brigade occurred in the zone of the 4th Infantry Battalion which is correspondingly Baljkovica, where a lot of the column went out. Counting all of the other individuals of the column who remained trapped inside of the Pobudje area, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and along the road there, as the military documents report, they're killing hundreds if not thousands of individuals from the column at that particular location in the Bratunac municipality. So there are two answers depending on which column element you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now talking about the victims of the column that was fighting. Is it true that at the very beginning, in the area of the Bratunac Brigade, Pobudje, the minefield, the shelling, there were several hundred casualties that were not buried, they remained on the surface.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding in both the Zvornik and the Bratunac municipalities is that because of the presence of many unmarked minefields and things of that nature, that the surface remains as we refer to, the people who died in the column both in Bratunac and Zvornik were not buried at all during the course of the conflict. Those remains remained on the surface and ultimately they began to be forensically collected after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I can agree about Pobudje, but do you have any proof that remains were collected from the surface in the area of Zvornik? My claim is that they were buried and they were not collected, and there were hundreds if not thousands of dead, and there were many more casualties in the area of Zvornik than in the area of Bratunac as you must know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to your first assertion, I don't know that that was done. I know that surface remains were recovered in the Zvornik area, and I know that many officers of the Zvornik Brigade were particularly concerned about going into minefields to retrieve dead bodies, particularly dead bodies of Muslim soldiers, and they weren't going to do that. I assume that Muslims who were killed in and around the combat positions of the 4th Battalion would have been removed, Baljkovica, the headquarters of the 4th Battalion, and buried at some location, and those numbers, given the ferocity of fighting on the 16 July, would have numbered some hundred. I don't know if I've ever seen an answer of how many were killed that day, and they were buried somewhere. So I think -- I said there is a great deal of forensics evidence with respect to individuals in various graves. I don't know where any surface remains of those individuals killed in the Zvornik municipality would be buried. I don't know if those have been discovered forensically yet or not, or whether those have been accounted for forensically.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very well. Can this be admitted, the transcript of the session of the Presidency of BH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2238, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I now ask -- just a moment, can we see 65 ter 01984. While we're waiting, Mr. Butler, when you were talking about killing in Bratunac on the 13th, do you mean the killing in a schoolhouse, some sort of gym hall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am talking about is that in the town of Bratunac on 13 July, there has been a good deal of information that individuals who were guarding Muslims at these various locations were taking these people and either in some cases individually or in small groups killing them at or near the locations where they were being detained. I believe that -- again, I don't follow the proceedings in this trial, but I believe that in previous cases there has been considerable testimony related to the sanitation people recovering bodies of those prisoners in the town of Bratunac on various days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only wanted to see what you meant when you say the massacre in Kravica. Did you establish what led to it? In fact, is it the case that you established that the atmosphere was very relaxed there, and in that atmosphere one prisoner approached a guard to ask for a light for his cigarette, and then he seized the soldier's rifle and opened fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, and nor was I asked to, establish a cause of that particular massacre or any particular massacre. I am aware of the story that relates to what may have triggered the massacre. I did not investigate that one way or another. My role again was to identify various military documents, which I did find, which shows that several members, I think two of the Special Police Unit at Sekovici and one of the Bratunac red brigade -- Red Berets unit were wounded at Kravica at approximately 1700 which I used to place that unit early on, the 2nd Sekovici unit, at that location at that time. Again I've heard the story. I do not know whether it's true or not. And of course I've heard the other part of the story, which is as a result of the injuries that those police officers received, that that was the predicate event which then led the police forces to begin firing into the warehouse, ultimately leading to the massacre. Frankly, it had been described as an impulse event, and I believe that if you look at the chronology of the killings, as well as the scope of what happened in the warehouse, that I do not believe that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, given the time we'll break now. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one quick matter. I think this may be obvious but I need to confirm it with the Court. Today is the day we would normally file our monthly witness list. In light of the fact that our previous filing encompassed all of the remaining witnesses, I presume that an additional filing is not necessary today. I spoke with Mr. Robinson. He agrees with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fair enough, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. Can I just inquire what the plan is for the rest of the day? I'm just thinking about timing. I will have some -- I think I will have some redirect, so I was just wondering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is that Mr. Butler may be -- may need to stay over the weekend, but -- do you think you can complete your cross-examination in the -- in the remainder of today, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I doubt it, Your Excellency. All the more so because Mr. Butler is putting for the his opinions on things, although he wasn't in Kravica. He just stated his opinion that he doesn't believe something that is obvious and confirmed, so I do have to deal with it in more detail. No. In fact, I'm sorry, I misspoke. Not his opinions, but his beliefs. Belief is something that depends on our will. We believe what we want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to rise now, but is my understanding correct, Mr. Butler, that you can stay -- you can be with us on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am available for testimony next week. I am at the indulgence of the Court, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break for an hour and resume at 1.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Morrison cannot be with us for this session due to his urgent matters, so we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 65 ter document 1984. The previous one should be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My learned colleagues have a look at this. Are you familiar with this document in which an order is issued to search the terrain on the 13th of July, to search the depth of the terrain? And under 3 it says that a white tape has to be used for markings for the purpose of identification.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it notes that under paragraph 5. I think you said 3 in the transcript, sir. But paragraph 5 notes that: "Men who participate in this search ... will wear a white band on their right shoulder as an identification mark." Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that our troops usually used such markings because our race and the race of our enemy at the time is the same? We had the same ethnic characteristics.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and in fact, many were even wearing the same former JNA uniforms, so as a result, one of the practices of the VRS was, was to -- in order to able to distinguish their troops from potential enemy soldiers was that their troops would wear various coloured ribbons or armbands on a particular sleeve to aid in battle-field identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2239, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have a look at the following document, 1D5536, and I'm not sure whether this can be a public document. I think there is a translation, but I'm not sure. Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see here on the 12th of July the Muslims intercepted a conversation. I'll read out the first part. It says the aggressor EIPED intercepted a conversation, recorded it between President Izetbegovic and the chief or the head of the municipality in Srebrenica, Avdic, on the situation in Srebrenica. In the private conversation we also found out that the aggressor EIPED has recordings of the conversation between President Izetbegovic and Naser Oric, but this is at 2000 hours. It says Goran Mauk [phoen] from the Serbian Army spoke about what is happening in Srebrenica at the time. He said, That's correct. Peace is abandoning Srebrenica, and this is what Osman Suljic asked for who -- he has been the president of the municipality up until now. This is a request because of the terror of Naser Oric's supporters, and he left Srebrenica a month ago at the same time when he ordered an attack on all Serbian positions. So he issued the order and fled around Srebrenica. He issued those requests to the Serbian troops, a request that the population should be allowed to leave peacefully, and this is being done. So the consequence of all these attacks ordered by Naser Oric and the ABiH as well as the NATO Air Force, the purpose of these attacks is the liberation of Srebrenica. And then he says, I'm gathering information on the civilian population and on the number of Muslim soldiers who surrendered and so on and so forth. And then he swears a little and he mentions the figure of 6.000, who are leaving towards the north, 6.000 civilians who are leaving by heading northwards. And then at 21 it says unidentified individuals, so I won't read that through.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page. [In English] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one in the middle, the paragraph in the middle. At 2100 hours, Boro Djurdjevic, a journalist from the Serbian Army, spoke to an unidentified person who couldn't be heard, and Boro Djurdjevic said the following: [As read] Everything has been completed. We had to do that. We regret the fact but, well, that's what happened. And then he says he left a month ago and then we wouldn't allow him to return. They are obviously referring to Oric. And then something is said about what happened. And towards the bottom at 1745 hours, the office of the president of the so-called Republika Srpska was called by a certain Mirko from abroad in order to convey information or to say that it was possible for him to inform the aggressor forces in advance of NATO attacks. He suggested if messages were obstructed again, they could be conveyed through Kipa, probably the Belgrade-Pale axis is concerned. Mirko doesn't speak Serbian very well, and the radio interceptors who followed him didn't think that English was his mother tongue either. Have you already seen this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I -- I may have. Particularly I recall the third part about the conversation with -- pertaining to Mirko and the fact that there was a belief that they could give early warning on potential NATO attacks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could it be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2240, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you could we now see 1D5087. Looks like we don't have a translation for this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you informed of these reports from the 2nd Corps command from the ABiH submitted to the ABiH Main Staff? It's on the fall of Srebrenica. The analysis was made on the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have seen this report before, but I'm fairly sure that it was not put in one of my -- my narrative reports.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read out the part where it says that an assessment was made according to which there would be a limited attack in order to take control of the road that the Chetniks could use for the needs of the mine. This was on the 6th of July, around 4.00, an all-out artillery and infantry attack was launched against the Srebrenica enclave and so on and so forth. Can we see the next page. So just as you did, they concluded that the task was to take control of the road; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusions are based on what the objectives are laid out in the Krivaja 95 plan, which is to reduce Srebrenica to the urban area. I don't believe that that corresponds to what's described here as what the ABiH believed was simply taking control of a road in order to access a mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope we'll have time to show a map from the agreement. I'll read out the part that concerns what they did here. In this part it says the command of the 28th Division knew about the existence of the tunnel. This is the tunnel that was entered by our sabotage troops, but they thought that it had been filled in. However, Becirevic designated several groups. From the 2nd Corps command and the General Staff, an order was issued stating that sabotage action should be taken to draw the attention the enemy and to carry out reconnaissance of the enemy in the depth. Becirevic designated several whose task was to carry out reconnaissance and to take action only if necessary, and all the groups carried out their task of reconnaissance without engaging in combat, and they all returned. One group set off in the direction of Kragivoda, and their task was to engage in combat. So on that occasion they destroyed one vehicle and killed three soldiers. One group was infiltrated in the Rupovo Brdo area. They also engaged in combat and killed four Chetniks. All sabotage and reconnaissance units from Zepa were issued the task to enter the Han Pogled, Han Pijesak, and Sokolac area and reach the Han Pijesak-Vlasenica road. According to the decision of the commander of the Brigade 285, nine groups were formed which carried out these tasks. These tasks engage in combat and killed about 60 Chetniks. One group entered the village of Visnjica and set fire to several houses. When these sabotage units returned from the Zepa area, the level of morale was raised in the area of Srebrenica and elsewhere. Two or three days before the units withdrew in the afternoon the command of the 28th Division was informed that they had broken through the defence line. Assistance was requested. And then the last sentence says heavy weapons that weren't surrendered to UNPROFOR were used throughout the combat period. One mountain gun remained at its gun emplacement. Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's very difficult to follow the line of questioning. What's the point of reading all this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't think I was going to read out that much. There are only a few things that have been marked that I wanted to read out, and these parts concern the attitude towards the civilians, and it also -- they also concern the contents of this report. Well, maybe I exaggerated a little with all these details. Could we scroll up. I'll skip something. It says given that the Chetniks at the time had already broken through to Zabojna [phoen], Sabovo [phoen], Srebrenica on the previous evening, the people broke into all the warehouses in the town. They took all the food reserves and head off in the direction of Potocari and panicked. That is where UNPROFOR troops sent them to under the pretext that they also had the intention of going to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did you notice that they took all the food reserves, and in fact it was said that there were no such food reserves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it wasn't part of my research to look at the issue related to the civilians moving up to Potocari in that respect. I don't know if they did or did not break into the various warehouses where food were stored and took them with them or not. I just have no way of knowing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the next page. It says almost all the civilian population - it's the second paragraph - almost all the civilian population from the town and surrounding villages set off on the 11th of July, 1995, around 1500 hours towards the main military base of UNPROFOR in Potocari, and by 2000 hours on at that day, about 20.000 refugees had gathered. Mr. Butler, can I remind you of a calculation? There were 20.000 in Potocari, 10- to 15.000 passing through the forests, and there was a total of 35.000. So let me remind you of those figures and do those figures tally now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it that the point that you're seeking to make is that there were a total of 35.000 people in the former enclave of Srebrenica, 20.000 of them went to Potocari, and that the column strength was between 10- and 15.000? Is that what you're -- okay. I agree again 10- to 15.000 is within a range of numbers that I believe is associated with the column. I think that the 20.000 figure is low for the number of civilians that went to Potocari. I believe that some of the Bosnian Serb military sources have a higher number than that, and I believe - excuse me - that the UN's count has an even still higher number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Should one trust the Muslim authorities? Should they know who is where? This is a report from the 2nd Corps. That was towards the end, two months -- or, rather, a month and a half after the event in question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I -- I don't trust anybody's numbers with respect to these types of estimates simply because I know that there are multiple numbers, each from what purports to be a reliable source. That's why normally you'll here me speak in ranges. So again I take your point that one would think that the military and civilian leadership in Srebrenica would have the most accurate numbers by virtue of being the civil, political control body for the Bosnian Muslim government in the enclave, but again I have to point out the fact that there are other numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at the following part where it says that although he wasn't an official representative of the civilian population, at 2215 Mandic was called to go to Bratunac for negotiations, and the Chetnik General, Mladic, was there on behalf of the Chetnik side. And then Ljubisav Simic, the leadership of the Bratunac Serbian municipality, Deronjic, and so on and so forth. Then it says it was suggested to the Chetniks that authorisation should be given for the evacuation of the civilian population under UNPROFOR escort to the free territory. Did you take this into consideration when you described the manner in which the population was moved out from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, setting aside this document, and perhaps going more authoritatively to the transcripts of the second meeting and the third meeting at the Hotel Fontana on the 11th and 12th of July, 1995, what was said in those meeting and the promises made in those meetings is part of the record. At this juncture, I trust that the Court has heard extensive testimony with respect to how those convoys departed Potocari, as well as the Dutch Battalion escorts that were initially escorting them and, over time, they lost the ability to do that. So I think those particular -- again, I never -- I don't characterise for the most part that movement. Again, I believe that there is more than ample information out there about that from more authoritative sources than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. Butler, but then I shouldn't be worried by the fact that at one point in time you used the term "deportation" and at another point in time you use the term "evacuation." You would leave this to others who dealt with civilians, wouldn't you? But the Defence is concerned, because in legal terms there's a difference between deportation and evacuation. But in any event, you did not concern yourself with the meaning of these terms, did you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware from a legal sense there is a difference in the phrase "deportation" and -- or "forcible transfer," as well as the term "evacuation." I understand that it is a legal issue that is before this particular Trial Chamber, so -- I mean, questions that I have been asked as to my opinion as to whether I believe that the Muslim population had a realistic chance to stay or not to stay, I believe I've already given answers to, and I don't believe that I'm the person who can qualify what the actual movement out of Potocari was in a legal sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Fair enough. Thank you. [Interpretation] Fair enough. Thank you. Can we see the next page. In the third -- or, rather, fourth paragraph it says on the night between the 11th and 12th of July, 1995, a decision was taken on breaking through in the direction of Tuzla. And then a little lower down it says the commanders were ordered to line up the units and to form a column. This was all on the night between the 11th and 12th of July, 1995. Then a little lower down it says that there were about 6.000 armed troops, not counting the troops from Zepa. And now let's have a look at the following passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up a little more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says that there were perhaps dozens of women. There weren't many women and children. Perhaps there were -- there was about a dozen women. As the column was moving forward, the commanders had received instructions. Amongst other things, they were instructed to leave the dead soldiers behind but to take the wounded with them. In the course of your work, did anyone emphasise the fact that the dead were to be left behind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I am aware that the -- what had in fact happened was that, of course, the wounded were carried forward where they could be and that the remains of soldiers or members of the column who had fell were left where they are. I don't know that anyone emphasised that, but I mean I'm aware that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I was conferring. No, I don't agree that this document be admitted, at least until -- I have no objection to it being marked for identification until we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2241, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D5527.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is a map on page 3. It's an integral part of the agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, and I won't ask to see whether it was necessary for Zepa and Srebrenica to be separated, but the road between them was to be free and under Serbian control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that it hasn't been released.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. It was reached on the 18th of April, 1993. An agreement reached between Mladic and Seferovic, the two generals. Can we see the next page. Here we can see the signatures. So this is an agreement on implementation. It's perhaps somewhat different in relation to the agreement reached on the 18th. Just a moment. Can we see the part that contains the map. I think it's page number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you see the signatures, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The signatures are on the original Your Excellency, but this is the English translation. The original is obviously in Serbian. It was signed by Gvero and some deputy of Halilovic's, Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that as far as Srebrenica is concerned, you can see the boundaries of the settlement, and these more regular lines mark those boundaries. Can you see the boundaries traced by these regular lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a boundary here that looks like a dotted and dashed line. I believe that's the boundary you're referring to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Do you see the village of Pusmulici to the south which is located outside those boundaries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you see that these two zones are separated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it what you're saying -- again, the village of Pilici [sic] is outside that designated area around the urban area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And to the south can you see the area that's been delimited there, and can you see that there's a free stretch of territory between those two areas, a stretch of territory that isn't included in this drawing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not tracking what you're -- which -- what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these two enclaves contiguous, or are they two distinct or separate enclaves? What would you say if you have a look at this map that is attached to the agreement on implementation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I'm only seeing one designated enclave or one designated area by that dotted and dashed line. I'm not seeing the second one. I mean, are you referring to in that case the area of terrain that's kind of diagonally crossed or -- I mean, I don't know what -- you're talking about a second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but is the enclave here attached to Zepa? Is the Srebrenica enclave attached to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, could this agreement on implementation together with the map be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. I was still just trying to find where the map is appended to the agreement, but I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You do not dispute the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not of the agreement, and this is a map which he has pulled. I haven't yet found that this map is actually attached to the same document signed by Gvero, which it was said that it was. I'm still looking at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I find it somewhat strange that the signature is lacking in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean -- at this point I do not have an objection. I may have some more comments on this agreement and map as I look into it. I do not believe we were notified of this map and document, so I'm a little bit behind in trying to figure it out, but at this time I don't object to its admission, but I may have a submission on it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: More specifically, my question was whether this is a draft or this is a signed agreement given that the signatures were lacking, but whatever the factual situation it was, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2242, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we briefly see P4491, which was admitted during your examination-in-chief. 4941. Sorry, I got the number wrong. It's a P number, P4941, a Prosecution exhibit. Page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde are marked here and delineated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There are -- there are delineated -- there are delineated lines in this that would reflect the former safe areas of -- or Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in on the right side, Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that on this map, too, we see clearly that the enclaves were not agreed to be joined? There is a passage between them, and the passage is under Serbian control.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the -- the fact is that the Srebrenica and the Zepa enclaves were considered to be by the United Nations separate enclaves. They were not one large enclave. The second one -- I mean, the presumption, obviously, is that if the enclaves are not under United Nations' control, that outside the territory, outside the enclave, would of course be Bosnian Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice in that report, the Muslim report on the fall, that Pusmulici village fell, but it wasn't even supposed to be in the area, because we see on the map it was supposed to fall outside the area. Do you agree, therefore, that the Muslim side expanded the area so much that Zepa and Srebrenica ended up being joined?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- again as I have testified, I am aware that there was a difference in opinion between certainly the VRS as -- and the United Nations as to what the actual demarcated boundaries of the enclave were. I do not know who was responsible for what ultimately would be the rough boundaries which correspond to where the United Nations' observation posts were, whether that was something that was Bosnian Muslims were behind or whether that was something that the UN themselves decided. Regardless of where the markings were, even though the enclaves were physically separated, the overall concern of the VRS is that military troops from the 28th Infantry Division at Srebrenica, as well as the brigade of the division in Zepa, did have constant communication back and forth and could travel through various paths and valleys back and forth between the Srebrenica and the Zepa enclave. So when you read in the military documents where the military is talking about the context of cutting the enclaves in two and separating the enclaves, what they mean in a military text or context is that they need to stop these Muslim military forces that are going back and forth between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I can just ask for some clarity, is Mr. Karadzic's case that on 2nd July, 1995, that there was only one large enclave, that the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves were not separate - and he referred to the village of Pusmulici being outside - is his case that Muslims were not allowed to live outside the boundaries of this -- of these two smaller enclaves and were not allowed to have villages or exist outside these enclaves, which is what it appears to be saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, we object to -- there's no need for Dr. Karadzic to state his case. He's putting questions to this witness on cross-examination, so we don't believe that he should be required to state his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We agree with Mr. Robinson. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to ask you, were you aware, did you familiarise yourself with the manipulations done with dead bodies when bodies were collected to be placed in other areas at a convenient moment? Are you aware that the Muslim side engaged in that sort of thing? It delayed the burials in order to be able to use these bodies in a different place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5192, please, is the next document I want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the translation does not appear, I'm sorry. Maybe page 2 is the translation. I see this has been used somewhere. There must be a translation. It seems to be accepted in this case as an MFI. This is dated 20th March. Look at paragraph 5 that begins with the date 27 March.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom in for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It talks about an attack by the Wasps who killed 12 Serbian fighters. It says they mounted an attack on the Vozuca front and on that occasion captured or killed 12 Serbian fighters. In a counter-attack by the VRS, the source claims they suffered losses of about 160 fighting men. They do not bury their fighters at cemeteries so that none of the families know about their relatives lost, and the hodzas prohibit funerals from being organised. This supports my thesis that bodies were manipulated. It says here that 160 fighters were killed there, and our intelligence service found out in March 1995 that these bodies had been relocated. Do you now see how it was possible to manipulate -- to manipulate the bodies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what -- what it says is that a source is that -- a source of information that they're reporting up is saying that. That is one isolated report of which I have no way to either confirm or deny. That is the belief of the source, and it's being reported up through the intelligence chain of the Drina Corps to the Main Staff. I don't know whether they even assign any credibility to that particular source or not. So it's just information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't put it to you that weapons were shipped from Iran via Split to the Tuzla airport.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is an MFI document, I'll call another one. Could we see 1D5190.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also from the intelligence section of the Drina Corps. They are informing the Main Staff, and it says confirmation was received that enemy forces from the 28th and 21st Divisions raised their combat readiness and are reinforcing their forces at the forward end. By active reconnaissance and scouting of our positions, they're trying to infiltrate sabotage groups among the disposition of our units. The units of the 28th Division are intensively scouting our positions and mounting sabotage actions against the firing positions of the artillery in order to cause fear, panic, and disorganisation in our ranks. And then it says we have unconfirmed information that the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica returned to the Muslims all the weapons that had been taken away from them, around 1500 rifles. It says the forces of the Dutch Battalion plan to recover the observation point in Zeleni Jadar by force by 14 June 1995. Did you have in your hands this document which speaks volumes about the preparations made and the co-operation between the 28th Division and the Dutch Battalion of the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I've seen this document before or not. Again, it's an intelligence report of intelligence information that's being passed on, and I would again remind you that according to the text of the report itself, they're not able to -- to even confirm the information that they're forwarding, and I'm not aware that the Dutch Battalion did, in fact, turn 1500 rifles over to the 28th Infantry Division in June of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Dutch Battalion offered it to them, but they refused, saying they had more modern weapons? And do you know that there were weapons shipments throughout the period of existence of the protected area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two separate questions. I am aware that approximately on the 9th or I believe it may even be as late as the 10th of July the issue was raised whether or not the weapons that were held by the UN should be returned to the Muslims. I don't know that they ever did that, because I think the Muslim position was no, they wanted the UN to defend them at that juncture. As to your second question, during the entire course of the existence of the enclaves, I believe it's well documented that Bosnian 2nd Corps did provide weapons. They were smuggled in over land through many known smuggling routes, ammunition, things of that nature. Again, as I've testified previously, the 28th Infantry Division, notwithstanding the disarmament agreement, was never disarmed and represented a military fighting force at the beginning of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we will be seeing each other again on Monday, we will go through that list which made you believe that the change from O to T was related to localities. But now I'd like to go through your summary. Could you please take a hard copy of your report. Maybe it will be easier. One of the first things in the first paragraph and the second paragraph, you say that the Muslim forces organised themselves very quickly after the Serbian action. Do you stand by that view that the Muslim forces started to organise themselves only after the Serbian attack, as you put it? It says facing the forces of Bosnian Muslims who quickly organised themselves. Do you know that the Muslim side had their own Patriotic League and organised their own forces even before the war began?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps if it would assist, if you could tell me which report and the number of the paragraph that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the revised narrative, the summary, paragraph number 1, year 2002.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which -- which paragraph again, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first one. You say that municipal Territorial Defence and later units of the VRS and commands that tried to expand the control of the Bosnian Serbs in that territory were facing the resistant forces of the Bosnian Muslims who were speedily organising themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters also cannot find this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you established when the Muslim armed forces were organised? Do you know that the decision to form the Patriotic League was made on the 30th March 1991, implemented on 30th April of 1991, and already in June every municipality had both a staff and a brigade in July 1991?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the specifics related to the establishment of the Patriotic League and various dates. I am aware that during 1991, many of the municipal organs split to reflect one for the Serbs and one for the Muslims during various points of time. So I mean that's as close as I can get to an answer. I don't know any of the details with respect to each municipality and by what dates what various staffs or brigades were established by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that only the Serbian side did not have an organised army, because it relied on the federal army, the JNA, to protect it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that somewhere around November/December of 1991, even while the JNA was still present in Bosnia, that there were various local Territorial Defence units that were set up and ultimately placed under the command of municipal Crisis Staffs. I do agree that of all three parties to the conflict, to the largest extent the Serb side believed that its interests in protected by the Yugoslav national army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 2 you say that in November, not long after the establishment of the Drina Corps, the VRS started a campaign of expulsion of Bosnian Muslims, including Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas. Does this look -- doesn't this look like a ready-made judgement, Mr. Butler? It certainly sounds like an indictment, but when you say it, then it also sounds like a judgement. A verdict. Why in November 1992 and the spring 1993, why didn't it start earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goal of my report, and even the part about the executive summary where the events of 1992 and 1993 are discussed, are simply to set the context so that the reader of the report would understand how all of the parties got to the month of July 1995, how the people who were scattered throughout Eastern Bosnia came to be in a United Nations enclave, how the military forces moved, where they were habitually assigned, and also reflects the various reports and the operations that occurred. Again, I'm not -- as I noted in my reports, I'm not writing a definitive history of the conflict in Eastern Bosnia. I am writing about the military aspects with respect to what happened in Srebrenica in 1995. There are -- there is a lot of context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was checking whether the LiveNote is working. It's working on the common drive but not in the personal computer, but we can continue. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I note that there is a lot of information with respect to what has happened in Eastern Bosnia from 1991 to July of 1995 that, I presume, the Trial Chamber has heard or will here that is not in my report, and that in and of itself would add many volumes to my report. But again, the limited goal that I undertook was simply to be able to set the context so that a reader of my narrative would understand in relatively short order how the situation in July 1995 was created.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My LiveNote is also not working, but I hope it will be repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Butler; am I to conclude that you did not study or establish the facts that are contained in your report and relate to the period before July 1995? Did you get interpretation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, sir. I was just waiting for -- it looks like there's some technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would it be okay to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, unless Mr. Butler is waiting for a check of the transcript. If my question has been interpreted and he's able to answer, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be a technical difficulties, so that the Registry cannot publish documents through e-court. Shall we take a brief break so that we can check? We'll rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 2.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, Mr. Butler, you did not study anything before July 1995. You only took this on in order to better understand July 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. While I have some history -- or have some of the historical background from Eastern Bosnia in there in the narrative, the primary focus of the narrative relates to the recounting of events for July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I will not challenge what you took from others. In order to better understand, I challenged it on prior occasions. Tell me, on what basis did you conclude that the killing in Cerska took place on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Cerska killing is a somewhat problematic date identification. It was in this context primarily testimonial based, and again, I used it simply to set the context. A particular witness who testified about seeing buses rolling down the Cerska Valley road, as well as earth moving equipment going in afterwards, and when one looks at that particular statement that we used and counted back the days, the conclusion was that it occurred on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. However, that was not proven in some other way. For instance, somebody being seen alive on the 17th of July and then found in an undisturbed grave.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I am aware of that, that there is DNA evidence that would conflict with that 13 July date. Again, that information was not available to anyone when that first estimate of the 13 July came out, and I do concede that an identification exactly when the Cerska grave was installed is problematic, at least as far as my review of military documents is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 4, chapter 4, you accepted that Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, on behalf of his superiors, asked for the withdrawal of the Dutch Battalion, the Muslim population, and Doctors Without Borders; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. I mean, I summarised that in 4.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 4.7 and 4.8, this is where you point out -- or, rather, you convey the transcript of the conversation between General Mladic and others at the second meeting, and then on the 12th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 4.7, I source that information in part from not only the tapes or the transcripts of those meetings -- the video-tapes of the meetings that were subsequently made into transcripts, I should say, but I also cite it to the report that the DutchBat commander sent to his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I go back to this topic, I wanted to ask you the following: Did you notice, for example, the daily reports that are sent from the brigade to the corps do not reach me in the same form? For example, also police reports. A lot of detail is lost by the time these reports reach the minister and then even more detail is lost if they're sent further up to me.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can -- on the military side, I believe it is clear that when one looks at the reporting from the brigades to the Drina Corps and then what is then ultimately incorporated to the Main Staff is obviously summarised. Part of the job of the staff is to select those topical issues which they believe are relevant that the higher headquarters needs to be aware of. With respect to the police reports, clearly we have the RD reports and the -- the RDB reports as well as the MUP reports from Vasic that are going at least to the police staff. I'm not sure I can comment on what information from the police staff or those reports that went directly to Mr. Kovac, what Mr. Kovac may or may not have relayed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree -- or, rather, have you established that POWs in Kravica were guarded by the police, not by the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that while there were some army soldiers present, the majority of the forces that were guarding the people in Kravica on 13 July 1995 were comprised of the 2nd Sekovici Detachment personnel and personnel from the 1st PJP company from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you seen a report about this event? It's more than an incident, so I'm not going to call it an incident. Did you see a report that was sent to anyone or me in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, just what's the incident? Because before we were talking about the wounding of the -- of Mr. Tudoric [phoen] and some of the Serb forces, or are we talking about the mass execution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to call it "event," the wounding and everything that happened after the wounding. So Mr. Nicholls is not going to be assisted by me in any way in formulating what this event was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not asking for formulating the event, and he's helped clarify it a bit. It's just if you say the incident at Kravica, the way the cross has gone that could have referred to several different things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see a report that was being sent to someone, or to me in particular, in order to provide me with this information about the dramatic happenings in the building of the cooperative in Kravica around 1700 hours?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that through the normal military reporting channels that either the army or the MUP reported that there was a massacre at Kravica at 1700 hours on the 13th of July, or in the case of the MUP that they were primarily responsible for it. There is that, of course, one written notation that comes well after the fact by Mr. Vasic, talking about the job that the first PJP company was involved in. So in that respect, given that there were no written reports that I'm aware of passed up either to the police or the army staffs, I don't know how you would have gotten that in a written form. Obviously I cannot speak to what verbally any individual in Bratunac may or may not have told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe my presence in Bratunac or Srebrenica in the month of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if you were in Bratunac or Srebrenica during the month of July 1995. I believe the first time that your presence is noted is as a result of a 2 August 1995 daily report from the Bratunac Brigade which reflects the fact that you and General Krstic were meeting in Srebrenica on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me correct you. It's just two days. On the 2nd of August I was in Drvar, and I tried to change the formation of the Main Staff into the staff of the Supreme Command, and it was on the 4th that I was in this region attending a religious ceremony; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I'll take your word at that. It's been a lot of years since I looked at that document, but I believe it's cited in my report, so it's easily verifiable one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at paragraph 5.7, where you say that Vasic, the chief of the CJB, that over 100 trucks have already been provided. Now it seems to me that the English translation says, "Have already been provided." And the Prosecution cares very much about the actual hours involved, whether it was after the third meeting at 10.00 or whether it was after 8.00 after the meeting in the Bratunac Brigade. However, now I'm going to ask the interpreters to confirm or deny this. When you say "obezbediti" in our language, doesn't that mean "secured"? So it was found out where it exists, but it hasn't actually been provided yet. So the information was that these 100 trucks exist. Do you see the difference between these two different meanings, between "secured" and "provided"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take your point with respect to at the time that Mr. Vasic was writing this report that there were not already 100 trucks on the ground at Bratunac. I think if you read that in conjunction with 5.5, it notes that all through the evening hours the Ministry of Defence, at the request of the army, had been looking to essentially secure and identify weeks that could be sent to Bratunac. In the case of any discrepancies in language, I would again, you know, invite the Court to go back to the original document. Like -- like I said yesterday, I'm at the mercy of CLSS with respect to English language translations from Bosnian Serb documents. So if there is any question about the discrepancy of the language, you know, please refer back to the original document I cite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I fully accept that, but quite simply that would be a major undertaking, because after all these are nuances in translation that are involved and meanings are quite different. But thank you at any rate. You see, 514 here. That is something that concerns me, although you have kindly said that you do not deal with qualifying the evacuation of the population. So this is what 514 says: "To support this continuing movement the Ministry of Defence issued an order on the 13th of July 1995 to the local Secretariat of Defence for the Bijeljina municipality," and so on and so forth. So let me ask you the following: On the basis of your experience and your theoretical knowledge, was this not a major risk for us, to have so many civilians, 20.000 civilians, relocated from their homes in a small area, in an area where personal revenge is highly likely?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is a risk. And as time goes on, it notes to be that. To mitigate that risk, many civilians from the local population were not permitted to enter Potocari on the 12th and the 13th, and there was a variety of military and police forces sent there also to ensure control. So while there are some instances individualistic killings in Potocari that occur on the 12th, in the evening of the 12th and the 13th, I don't believe they compare in number to the same types of individualistic killings that you see in and around Bratunac that is occurring where there are less military and police forces to guard the prisoners and that the local population has freer access to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will stop here today. You have spent almost the same time as the Prosecution did for its examination-in-chief, all be it minus five or nine minutes. How much more would you need on Monday to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellencies, taking into account the reports, although Mr. Butler has just made things easier for me now that I focus only on July 1995, because that is his authentic research, so I would really like to have two sessions if that would be possible. I think that would be a very good thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber will give you a session on Monday. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll need to move into private session for a request related to a filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second we're still in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise for this week and resume on Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of April, 2012, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
